speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: asked the Minister for Health (a) what eligibility criteria will determine access to subsidised Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) consultations under Healthier SG; (b) whether medical certificates issued by TCM practitioners will be accepted; (c) what quality assurance measures will ensure TCM treatments within Healthier SG meet the required standards; and (d) what steps will be taken to boost Healthier SG enrolment among older residents, including through partnerships with TCM practitioners.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I will invite Members to seek clarifications at the end of my answer, if need be.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If the questions have been addressed, it may not be necessary for them to proceed with the questions for future Sittings.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our effort will focus on two areas: first, for preventive care under Healthier SG; and second, for acute settings in hospitals.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: About 20% of Singapore residents aged 40 and above visit TCM practitioners every year.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: TCM clinics are hence, useful touch points to engage residents to join Healthier SG and practise good preventive care.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I mentioned in the speech that under Healthier SG, health screening, vaccinations, chronic disease management, being Western medicine interventions, will have to be performed by general practitioners (GPs).

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Where TCM practitioners can play a useful role is lifestyle changes, given the holistic approach to health in TCM.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MOH will consult Western doctors and TCM practitioners on how they can collaborate to care for our residents.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The training and support for TCM practitioners under Healthier SG will depend on the eventual model of collaboration.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: A fruitful collaboration should lead to an increased uptake of preventive care, such as screenings and vaccinations, as well as adoption of healthier lifestyles among Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: At present, under the Employment Act, employers are legally required to recognise medical certificates issued by registered medical or dental practitioners after proper clinical assessment for the purposes of granting paid sick leave.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Although TCM practitioners are not registered medical and dental practitioners under the Act, employers have the discretion to also recognise medical certificates issued by them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If and when we decide to do so in a public hospital setting, proper referral and review protocols will be established, no different from the integration of medical subspecialties that are ongoing.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: So, when will the accreditation framework be in place to identify qualified TCM practitioners within Healthier SG?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Will employers be required to accept medical certificates (MCs) from these accredited practitioners?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Because this could assure Singaporeans who prefer using TCM, that their medical choices will be recognised and respected.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can patients be given more flexibility to combine TCM and Western treatments, especially for chronic conditions, and receive government subsidies or use MediSave for both treatments?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This could allow the preventive and lifestyle-focused approach of TCM to complement Western interventions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Lastly, could MOH facilitate opportunities for TCM practitioners and Western-trained doctors to receive some cross-disciplinary exposure and training in each other's medical principles, as is done in places, like China and Taiwan?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This could foster mutual respect, encourage collaboration and strengthen confidence in each other's standards.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I did not realise there are four questions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, I am now trying to take stock what are they.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The first question is about accreditation, when will it be done?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are taking a very practical approach here.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: All round the world including in China, the regulatory system is a Western-centric one.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But TCM, on the other hand, lots of people use it, I agree.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But if we say let TCM be regulated under today's healthcare regulatory regime, I think it will wither and die because the Western regulatory system is just not compatible with TCM.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Therefore, we take a practical approach to say "take you out of the system and you self-regulate" and then you can thrive.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: You are allowed self-regulation, you can thrive, you can serve a quarter of Singaporeans but some of these privileges, including recognition of MCs, do not follow.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But what I mentioned earlier, if there is accreditation and people are confident of TCM practitioners' assessment, employers are free to exercise discretion to recognise them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The next two questions are what I had addressed in my speech recently and in my reply.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There is now a lot of research, scientific research on TCM.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And some of them, I think if we can study them and ensure that they are safe, efficacious, cost-efficient, we can start to integrate them into our mainstream regulatory system, mainstream healthcare system, including the management of chronic disease.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As we do so, it is quite an involved process.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, we are taking this step by step and as we do so, I think they will also learn from each other, which is a good thing.
